function.name: run_tests

reasoning_details.text:
I'm thinking through the L2-at-end mechanism for M/L on B200: since outputs use evict_last, they accumulate in L2 as the kernel runs, and once L2's 126MB fills with evict_last output lines, newer writes start displacing older ones out to memory.

I'm also considering whether input loads should use evict_first versus default caching policy to free up more L2 space for outputs -- though a similar approach on A100 (evict_first loads with evict_last stores) actually performed worse. I wonder if loads tagged as "last use" (which behave like evict-first) might work differently on B200, and whether the roughly 126MB of free dirty output space at the end of the kernel could meaningfully reduce memory traffic for the L band spanning 400–800MB.

I'm also realizing the harness's zero-filled buffer creates 126MB of dirty lines sitting in L2 at kernel start, and every line we allocate for our own data evicts one of these dirty zero lines, forcing an unavoidable writeback -- which adds extra traffic inside our timing window that I hadn't accounted for.

With evict_last on outputs, the harness's normal-priority dirty lines and our normal-priority inputs get evicted first, so by the end roughly 126MB of outputs remain cached while the harness writebacks get absorbed into the total -- meaning effective DRAM traffic converges to something like reads plus final outputs rather than reads plus all writes. For the 100MB workload case with 50MB reads and 50MB writes, I'm checking whether evict_last keeps enough of those output bytes resident in L2 to meaningfully reduce the traffic we actually pay for.

For L, once outputs exceed 126 MB the harness dirty lines all get evicted regardless, so total writes converge to the same value as before — meaning evict_first mostly helps M, not L. I'm also second-guessing this against the A100 result where evict_first loads plus evict_last stores showed a +4.3% gain for L, but A100's L2 is a different size (40 MB) so the mechanism may not transfer directly — since evict_first lines are preferred eviction targets ahead of normal-priority harness lines, new allocations should evict...

Even accounting for fixed overhead, the implied bandwidth comes out around 11 TB/s, which is impossible on this hardware. So either the zero-fill lines in L2 aren't actually treated as dirty (perhaps Blackwell's L2 compression handles zero lines specially), or the write-back is happening lazily rather than synchronously within the measured window.

Looking at the numbers: 100 MB parent takes ~16.4 µs, and if reads alone (50 MB) hit DRAM at 8 TB/s that's 6.25 µs. Subtracting the fixed 3 µs overhead gives 13.4 µs for 100 MB, implying ~7.5 TB/s effective — which is suspiciously close to peak 7.05 TB/s, maybe a 6% discrepancy that's hard to pin down without more data. It's unclear whether all the writes are actually reaching DRAM or just some fraction of them, so I'm stuck trying to cleanly separate reads from writes in this measurement.

I want to think about what levers I actually have: whether EF loads versus EL stores behave differently on B200 (untested, risky), whether processing order matters for which rows stay cached (probably not controllable), or whether I could discard L2 lines for input data after reading them — since inputs are clean, invalidating them after use would free slots without write-back, making them preferred eviction targets over the harness's dirty lines, which could reduce unwanted write traffic.

But I'm now worried about discard semantics — the spec says the memory contents become undefined after discard, which would be dangerous if the line is dirty. Since the harness copies inputs into the pool right before each call, those input lines might actually still be dirty in L2 at the start of the kernel, so discarding them could corrupt the real input data rather than just dropping a clean cached copy.

I should check the timing harness's actual ordering: does it flush L2 before or after copying inputs, since that determines whether discard is safe to use on input addresses. If the flush happens after the copy, the inputs would mostly be evicted to DRAM already, making a later discard reckless and not worth the risk — so I'll set that idea aside and move to other avenues like reducing CTA count for larger per-thread loads, or examining B200's split L2 partition behavior and how addresses map to partitions.

Store writes themselves look fine — each 256-bit store writes a full 32-byte sector, and four lanes together write a complete 128-byte line, so there's no partial-write waste. The real lever is thinking about which lines are worth keeping in L2 at the end: only the dirty output lines matter, since inputs become useless after being read, but evicting dirty lines forces a costly write-back unless compression kicks in — and Ampere's compute data compression in L2 needs explicit allocation attributes that PyTorch doesn't use by default. So minimizing eviction cost on dirty output lines seems like the key constraint to work around.

With normal LRU behavior, the harness's dirty lines are older and get evicted first by new input allocations, so under a standard policy a 100 MB workload ends up evicting ~100 MB of harness dirty lines as write-back. But using evict-first on loads changes that: input lines recycle among themselves instead of competing with harness lines, so harness dirty evictions shrink down closer to just the output bytes — potentially saving tens of megabytes of write-back traffic compared to the default policy.

Actually under pure LRU, the last 126 MB allocated should cover all inputs and outputs for a 100 MB workload, meaning evict_last shouldn't matter at all for M. But it still gained 7–9%, which suggests the L2 isn't behaving as pure LRU—maybe its replacement or write policy differs from that assumption.

I'm wondering if the zero-fill memset behaves like streaming/evict_first stores, pushing harness lines out early and letting evict_last on outputs protect them from eviction by inputs. But since 100 MB fits under 126 MB, that shouldn't matter either—unless the L2's effective capacity is split across partitions (e.g., each partition only 63 MB), so data duplicated or accessed cross-partition effectively halves usable cache, which would explain the gain.

If so, at M (100 MB allocations) that reduced effective capacity would cause LRU eviction of early outputs, and evict_last would specifically protect them—matching the gain pattern I'm seeing. With EF loads for inputs, those would be preferentially evicted too, leaving more cache room for outputs at the end. For the larger L case, the cache is already saturated with evict_last outputs regardless, so EF loads shouldn't change the final state much, just reduce interference—yet A100 showed L performing 4.3% worse with EF loads, which is puzzling since EF shouldn't block the load itself; maybe it's interfering with prefetching or sector promotion.

Maybe L2 retention isn't perfect since inputs also compete for cache space. If outputs were fully retained at 126 MB, I'd expect traffic around 680 MB giving ~99 µs, but the measured 115.9 µs implies actual traffic closer to 796 MB — meaning only about 9 MB of savings, far less than hoped.

Comparing cases without hints to L-level hints shows only a 2-4% gain, which is modest. Looking at M-band numbers (100MB and 201MB), the implied bandwidth comes out around 7.5 TB/s with a 3 µs fixed overhead assumption.

Given this uncertainty, I'm leaning toward testing the EF-loads-plus-EL-stores hypothesis on B200 since it's grounded in solid L2 reasoning, and checking it against the list of already-proposed ideas (bulk1d ring, tokblk, l2pf, token-r2, sw2-disp, wstat-pf2) — it doesn't seem to overlap with any of those.

But the r5 results actually tested EF loads with EL stores on A100 and found a 4.3% regression, leading to rejection there. A100 has a smaller L2 (40MB) and uses 128-bit loads though, whereas B200 could use 256-bit evict-first loads without needing a cache-hint register, and I recall CAKE found this approach favorable on B200 specifically. I'm also considering whether a no-allocate L1 combined with evict-first L2 prefetch could help, or other eviction policy variants like evict-unchanged, though these feel like long shots. Discarding L2 lines for inputs seems too risky since it could lose dirty input data if the harness just copied it in.

I'm wary of applying priority demotion to evict-normal since it doesn't seem useful, and I'm weighing whether to trust the A100 proxy given it's the only measurement we have, despite B200 likely behaving differently due to cache size and load width differences. I'm also toying with a fractional eviction policy idea, and thinking about what ends up occupying L2 near the end of execution as another angle to explore.

The real opportunity seems to be in reducing harness dirty writeback costs — since input lines are read once, using evict-first loads lets each new input eviction clear out a clean previous input line instead of forcing a costly dirty writeback, which could meaningfully cut traffic at larger memory sizes. I don't have confirmation whether the A100 session's earlier gains held across all three memory tiers, so it's unclear if that +4.3% L result generalizes well given A100's smaller L2 capacity.

Could also be instruction overhead from the cache hint rather than a real memory effect. I'd really want to test this directly on A100, but its 40MB L2 doesn't represent the M regime well — H200's 50MB L2 would be a better testbed, though that's not available here.

There's no clean alternative that avoids priority games to reduce harness-dirty evictions. I could try the `.L2::evict_first` qualifier on 256-bit loads with the nc (non-coherent read-only) path, since ptxas 12.9+ supports this combination and the inputs are read-only anyway.

Looking at the measured data: r2 with evict_first loads/stores was 4-5% slower than r3 with no hints, likely from the evict_first stores specifically. The g2 vs d1 comparison on Triton shows mixed signal across sizes (S faster with hints, L slower), so these effects are confounded and I can't cleanly isolate just the evict-first loads' contribution. Given A100 showed a 4.3% regression on large sizes and the expected value calculation looks marginal, I'm skeptical this is worth pursuing further without a cleaner isolated test.

Another angle worth considering is boosting memory-level parallelism, though the existing proposals already touch on that. I'm also wondering about partition behavior on B200's L2 with full eviction fraction, and whether a shape-based policy — using evict-last only for the tail portion of output tiles near the L2 capacity boundary, normal elsewhere — would end up in the same steady state anyway since inputs get evicted before the evict-last outputs regardless.

But I'm realizing the real problem: early outputs marked evict-last clog the cache with dirty lines, and when later outputs need room, there's nothing left to evict except those already-dirty evict-last lines, forcing write-backs each time new output space is needed — so the mechanism doesn't actually help the way I'd hoped.

In the L band, everything eventually gets evicted with that 126 MB write-back being unavoidable unless allocations fit within free plus EF-recycled lines. Once outputs and harness fill the cache, further allocations evict harness before EL outputs, so harness ends up fully evicted in L; in M with 50 MB outputs, EF loads cut harness eviction to 50 MB versus 100 MB without, and in the 100 MB output case it's 100 vs 200 capped at 126.

Testing the 100 MB case: with 50 MB reads plus 100 MB harness write-back under pure LRU, I'm getting 13.4 µs implying 11 TB/s, which is physically impossible — so my assumption that harness lines are dirty in L2 must be wrong, or the write-backs are happening at a different point than I think. Maybe the zero-fill via cudaMemsetAsync still writes through L2, or perhaps dirty lines get flushed eagerly when DRAM is idle, or the ordering between input copies and the L2 persist-cache reset is different than I assumed.

If the input copies actually happen after the flush, inputs would still be warm in L2 despite being described as always cold — and if zero-filled outputs are written after the flush too, those dirty output lines could already sit in L2 when my kernel starts, letting my stores hit without allocating from DRAM. I can't pin down the actual ordering, but the 7.5 TB/s fit suggests some write traffic really is being avoided, and the eviction-first load hypothesis still gives a coherent L2-occupancy story — I'm trying to figure out if there's a safer alternative explanation, like no-allocate load hints, before committing to it.

I'm also considering whether to apply evict-first loads only for the mid-size band and leave the large band using the original behavior, since the size can be dispatched via a runtime policy argument rather than needing separate kernels — though I'm unsure whether evict-first would actually help at the large size, since it depends on how much of L2 the inputs still occupy by the end under the current approach.

EF line recycling benefits depend on how early EF-tagged lines appear per set, since allocations only pick them as eviction targets once present. The gains seem modest at S but real, so I'm landing on the design labeled r6-ldg256-os-r16-efld as my working configuration.

I want the dispatch logic to apply EF loads for token counts up to around 2100 and fall back to the parent path otherwise, but I'm debating whether to include S in that range or keep it isolated to avoid confounding effects. The target band covers M and L, and theory suggests L should be neutral to this change, so maybe a single uniform dispatch threshold is the safest choice rather than trying something special for L given the uncertain A100-to-B200 regression behavior.

I realize A100's S-band results can act as a proxy for B200's M band given similar L2 cache ratios, so I can run the all-EF variant on A100 across the 25-200 MB range to approximate B200's M and L behavior, then scale the dispatch threshold by the L2 ratio. Now I'm writing the kernel template with the EF_LD boolean parameter...

Writing cache hint policy logic...

compile_b200

reasoning_details.text:
EF loads actually hurt on A100 at large sizes, showing an 8.5% regression, with no benefit at small sizes—so the harness dirty eviction theory doesn't pan out there, and I should abandon it. The hurt might stem from EF lines getting evicted before other sectors in the line are fetched, but I'm not certain; let me consider the inverse approach instead.

I'm wondering whether mixing eviction policies—evict_first for early tiles, evict_last for the tail—might explain things, but EF stores already measured poorly in r2, so that's probably not it. Maybe the win is really about EL outputs dodging victim status while harness-dirty lines and inputs get evicted instead. With limited GPU calls left, I should prioritize testing the most promising lever rather than chasing more theories.

Thinking about what actually bounds throughput at 805 MB over 115.9 µs: CTA turnover and bytes-in-flight per SM seem like the real constraint, since each CTA only loads once before exiting. With 49152 CTAs spread across SMs in waves of 8, increasing bytes per thread (already proposed) seems like the natural fix rather than restructuring CTA size, since thread count alone doesn't raise bytes in flight. I'm also considering whether interleaving Q and K tiles in the grid ordering could improve DRAM page locality by having concurrent CTAs touch overlapping memory regions.

Looking at the write side, evict_last stores should accumulate dirty lines and flush on eviction, which seems fine. At the end, the L2 should mostly hold evict_last outputs since normal-priority inputs get evicted first, but I'm unsure whether there's a hardware cap limiting how much of the cache can hold evict_last lines simultaneously on Ampere.

Given the persisting L2 carve-out might default to zero, the createpolicy evict_last hints could actually be getting treated as normal priority, which would mean r5's improvement is coming from somewhere else entirely. Since the L-hint behavior seems inverted on A100 compared to expectations, I should try alternative load hints instead.

Maybe it's worth pivoting to a structural change like warp-level Q/K interleaving. The DRAM bandwidth numbers suggest reads-only streams beat mixed read+write, so deferring writes to stay in L2 could help, but the retention ceiling at L seems fixed around 126 MB.

I'm also considering CTA scheduling overhead — with 49152 CTAs of 256 threads launched in one shot, I should check the CTA launch rate.

Each CTA's lifetime seems bounded by DRAM load latency plus compute and store/exit overhead, and working through the numbers (8 resident CTAs, bytes in flight per SM) gets surprisingly close to the observed throughput. This points to needing more bytes in flight per SM — maybe by having each thread load two rows instead of one, doubling in-flight bytes, though that changes occupancy given register pressure.

I'm also considering alternatives that don't cost registers: prefetching the next tile's rows into L2 explicitly, or staging through shared memory with async bulk copies — though that TMA approach already tested worse.

I'm also weighing a scheme where each half-warp loads both a Q row and a K row for the same head, doubling in-flight bytes per thread at a modest register cost, though it's close enough to the existing "two rows per thread" idea that I'm wary of it counting as a repeat.

Separately, I'm puzzling over why EF loads hurt by 8.5% on A100 — maybe it's not about which lines get evicted but about sector-level DRAM access granularity, where EF hints could cause lines to be evicted before all sectors of a 512B contiguous load arrive and merge across requests.

I consider testing loads with the L2::256B prefetch qualifier as an alternate explanation, and briefly entertain whether varying the EL fraction for stores (constant vs tail-only) could explain the gap, but conclude the dirty EL lines would get evicted equivalently either way, so that angle isn't promising.

I turn to a pairing idea instead: pack Q+K together so each thread handles 64B in flight, with a CTA covering 16 rows of both Q and K, which also cuts CTA count and launch overhead. Adding the extra weight loads (wq, wk) pushes register use to roughly 48, giving about 5 CTAs/SM, 1280 threads, and 80KB in flight — worth checking against the occupancy limits.

Trying launch_bounds at 6 CTAs per SM to cap registers around 42, might risk spilling. This Q/K pairing plus deferred weight loading approach should be distinct from the existing ldg256-token-r2 variant, so I'll test it on A100 with fallback 128-bit loads. One catch: pairing halves the CTA count, which could hurt the smaller S workload since tile counts drop from 768 to 384 — I'll template a PAIR flag to toggle this and move forward with writing it.

reasoning_details.text: With 32 registers and no spilling, I can fit 8 CTAs per SM, giving 2048 threads and 128 KB in flight. I'll go with that and test the final version using (256,8).

It's odd that forcing 8 CTAs on A100 actually runs slower than the natural 39-register, 6-CTA case—likely because the A100's fallback path uses different, less efficient load instructions, so pushing occupancy higher there doesn't help since the in-flight requirement is already low. On B200, though, the 32-register version avoided any spills entirely, which probably explains why that platform doesn't see the same penalty.

Given the uncertainty around whether B200's benefit outweighs A100's small slowdown, I'll go with the risk-averse choice: submit the 39-register, 6-CTA version I already validated in my first test run, since it was neutral on A100 and still provides solid occupancy on B200. I'll keep its code and comments as-is since it's already been checked, then move on to writing the design card.
